title: Even Arjuna forgot
hookLine: after the war, Arjuna admits he's forgotten the Gita, and why Hindus study scripture every day
carry: svadhyaya: study the sacred words daily

cards: The war is over. The Pandavas have won, at a terrible cost, and Yudhishthira rules as king. One day Arjuna and Krishna are spending time together in the palace, and Arjuna admits something astonishing.
Remember what you taught me before the battle? I've forgotten it. Tell me again.
The man who heard the Gita from Krishna himself, on the field, has lost it.

teach.b: This is in the Mahabharata, in a book after the war, the Ashvamedhika Parva. Krishna isn't pleased. He says he taught it in a state of yoga, and he can't simply say it all again the same way.

So he teaches him again, in other words, a teaching called the Anugita, the song after. Teachers draw a plain lesson from it: hearing once, even from God, isn't enough. That's why Hinduism has svadhyaya.
Sva, your own; adhyaya, study, recitation. Your own regular study of sacred words. The Gita names it among the divine qualities, and in its discipline of speech.
The Taittiriya Upanishad's teacher tells the student who is leaving: don't neglect your study. The yoga tradition counts it among its core observances. So Hindus keep rhythms for it.
Some read a chapter a day, finishing the Gita in eighteen days, then start again. Some read a few verses each morning.
Many temples and homes celebrate Gita Jayanti, the Gita's birthday, in the month of Margashirsha, often with a full recitation.

teach.h: A VERSE A DAY, A CHAPTER A DAY.
teach.b: And the same verse says different things in a different year; the Gita itself keeps returning to letting go of the fruit, in chapter two, three, five and eighteen.
Svadhyaya isn't homework you finish. It's how the words stay alive in you, so a line turns up uninvited, halfway through a hard phone call.

how: Many Hindus read or recite the Gita regularly: a few verses each morning, a chapter a day across eighteen days, or a full recitation on Gita Jayanti in the month of Margashirsha; svadhyaya, one's own study of sacred texts, is counted as a spiritual discipline.

games.q: you're Krishna. the war is over, and Arjuna says: I've forgotten everything you taught me. what do you do?
o: teach him again, in other words.
repeat all seven hundred verses word for word.
games.why: the Anugita: Krishna says he can't repeat it the same way, and teaches him again.

practice: Take your verse from yesterday. If you pray, say it once before a picture of God or a lamp, the way many Hindus begin the day. If you don't, just say it once, slowly.
Then picture tomorrow, waking, the hardest hour, the drive home, and place the verse somewhere in that day, like a note in a coat pocket. Arjuna forgot; you're leaving yourself a way back.

wordCard.voice: Svadhyaya, one's own study: reading and reciting the sacred words again and again, because even Arjuna forgot.

orig.note: Sanskrit: svadhyaya, one's own (sva) study or recitation (adhyaya) of sacred texts; Gita 16.1 and 17.15.

carryVoice: Your line: svadhyaya: study the sacred words daily. Even Arjuna needed to hear it twice. Until tomorrow.
